entry.title: Building a Movie Recommendation API with Spring Boot 🎬
entry.summary:
Recently I built a backend API for a movie and TV show recommendation platform using Java and Spring Boot. The goal of the project was to practice designing a REST API, implementing authentication, and integrating an external API. The API includes several features: Search movies and TV shows using the TMDB API User authentication with JWT Save favorite movies and shows Rate content Get trending content RESTful API design API documentation using Swagger / OpenAPI Java 21 Spring Boot Spring Security JWT Authentication Spring Data JPA PostgreSQL TMDB API (The Movie Database) Swagger / OpenAPI Example request to get trending content: GET /content/trending
Example response: { "page": 1, "results": [ { "title": "War Machine", "release_date": "2026-02-12", "vote_average": 7.1 } ] }
The application follows a layered architecture: Controller → Service → Repository → Database
This structure helps keep the code organized and maintainable. The API is documented using Swagger / OpenAPI, which makes it easy to explore and test the endpoints. While building this project I practiced several backend concepts: Designing REST APIs Implementing authentication with Spring Security Using JWT for authorization Integrating external APIs Structuring a backend project using layered architecture You can find the full project here: https://github.com/alejandrotg-code/tv-and-movie-db Feedback and suggestions are always welcome!

entry.title: Escaping the Buffer: The Advanced Guide to Streams in Node.js & Next.js
entry.summary:
Escaping the Buffer: The Advanced Guide to Streams in Node.js & Next.js
If you have been writing JavaScript for a few years, you are probably intimately familiar with async/await. It makes asynchronous code look synchronous, keeps the event loop unblocked, and is universally loved. But async/await hides a massive system design bottleneck: Buffering. If you are building data-intensive applications — proxying AWS S3 uploads, generating massive CSVs from MongoDB, or rendering complex Next.js Server Components — relying solely on buffered data will inevitably lead to Out of Memory (OOM) crashes and abysmal Time to First Byte (TTFB).
